kicker: THE FILES · AFTER THE CIVIL WAR, 1865–1972
label: Lost the story
title: The Civil War Ended in 1865. The Fight Over the Textbooks Didn’t.
dek: In 1861 the Confederacy’s founders wrote down that secession was about slavery. After the war, its veterans told a different story: the South fought for states’ rights, and enslaved people had been content. In 1920 they asked for a rulebook to grade history textbooks. Virginia’s state textbooks were still calling slave life “generally happy” until 1972.
summary: How Confederate veterans recast the Civil War as a states’ rights fight and put the ‘happy slave’ into Southern textbooks, taught in Virginia to 1972.

blocks.text: Company E, 4th U.S. Colored Infantry · Fort Lincoln, D.C. · November 1865 · William Morris Smith / Library of Congress
1861 · The record · The Confederacy, in its own words. Mississippi’s official declaration of why it was leaving the Union, months before the war began:
“Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery.”
1881 · The rewrite · Twenty years later. Jefferson Davis, president of the Confederacy during the Civil War, in his own history of the war:
Slavery “was in no wise the cause of the conflict, but only an incident.”
Before the Civil War and after it, both in their authors’ own words. This story is about how the second version got into Southern schoolbooks, and stayed.
Lesson I · A sentence with a past

In 1957, every eleventh grader in Virginia’s public schools read the same state-written history book. It said an enslaved person “did not work as hard as the average free laborer, since he did not have to worry about losing his job. In fact, the slave enjoyed what we might call comprehensive social security.”
Mississippi’s 1861 declaration of the causes of secession.

That line sounds like something a textbook committee made up. Versions of it had been in print for a century. In 1857 the Virginia writer George Fitzhugh, a leading defender of slavery, called enslaved Southerners “the happiest, and, in some sense, the freest people in the world.” In 1918 Ulrich B. Phillips, the top slavery historian of his day, pictured plantations as kindly places and brushed aside what formerly enslaved people said about their own lives.

Generations of Americans learned the same story. The South fought for states’ rights. Its generals were gentlemen. It lost because it was outnumbered, not because it was wrong. In 2011 the Pew Research Center asked what the Civil War was mainly about. Forty-eight percent said states’ rights. Thirty-eight percent said slavery.

The Confederacy’s own founders would have been confused. Its vice president, Alexander Stephens, said the new government’s “corner-stone rests upon the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man.”

So the easy version of this article is a villain story: liars rewrote history, and the country fell for it. The true version is harder. It’s about a country tangled up in slavery’s money from its first budget, Northerners who hated slavery and didn’t much like Black people either, and a peace that had to be built after a war that killed an estimated 750,000 people. The happy slave was the piece that made that peace feel clean.

The story, spread by Confederate veterans and their families after 1865, that the South fought for states’ rights rather than slavery, that slavery had been kind, and that the Confederacy lost only because it was outnumbered.

Sections tabbed ◆ The Price of Peace follow one argument, made by historians such as David Blight and Nina Silber: that the “happy slave” made the reunion of white North and South feel clean. The last pages weigh it, including the strongest case against it.
We quote sources exactly, including offensive words, so you can see what was actually said.
Lesson II · The founders did the math on slavery.

In 1783 the new United States was broke. Congress could only send each state a bill, so it decided to split the costs by population. That raised a question with a dollar sign on it: how do you count people who are held as property?

James Madison kept private notes of the debate. On March 28, 1783, the South Carolina delegate John Rutledge offered to “rate Slaves, as 2 to 1.” Then Madison said he “wd. propose that Slaves should be rated as 5 to 3.”

Three-fifths. Congress adopted it on April 18, 1783, and four years later it went into the Constitution, this time for both taxes and seats in the House. It was never a statement that a person was three-fifths human. It was a bookkeeping rule. The fight was over who paid, and later over who got power.

The Constitutional Convention haggled in the same terms. On August 22, 1787, the Pennsylvania delegate Gouverneur Morris suggested sending the slave trade, export taxes and shipping laws to one committee. “These things,” he said, “may form a bargain among the Northern & Southern States.”
A BOOKKEEPING RULE. The three-fifths ratio was set in 1783 to split the costs of the war and of government. In 1787 it went into the Constitution for both taxes and seats in the House. Illustration.

The deal let the slave trade run until 1808. In exchange, Northern states got easier rules for passing shipping laws. In 1788 the Maryland delegate Luther Martin, who sat on that committee, described it in print: the North, “notwithstanding their aversion to slavery,” gave the South “a temporary liberty to prosecute the slave trade” in return for “no restriction on navigation acts.”

Historians still argue about what this means. Sean Wilentz of Princeton points out that the delegates kept the words “slave” and “property” out of the text on purpose. Other historians say the bargain mattered more than the wording. Both sides agree on the text. The word “slave” never made it into the Constitution. A tax of up to ten dollars “for each Person” imported did.
Lesson III · By 1860, slavery was too big to buy out.
By 1860 about four million Americans were enslaved. The economic historian Roger Ransom puts their market value at close to $3 billion, about three-quarters of a year’s national output.

In the South, enslaved people were also the credit system. Two Louisiana banks alone took about 13,000 enslaved people as collateral for loans, according to a 2005 disclosure by JPMorgan Chase, which later absorbed them.
1862: Lincoln asks Congress to help pay any state that ends slavery. No slaveholding state took the offer.

The National Park Service puts it this way: the value of enslaved people was greater than the invested value of all the nation’s railroads, factories and banks combined. One is a sale price and the other is money put in, but the comparison still shows the scale.

rows: the market value put on them, by the economic historian Roger Ransom’s estimate
of all the wealth in the country

blocks.text: Other countries had bought their way out. In 1833 Britain paid slave owners in its colonies £20 million and freed more than 800,000 people. But those colonies were far away and a small part of Britain’s economy. The economist Claudia Goldin figured that even an American buyout spread over 25 years would have tripled federal spending.

And the owners weren’t selling. In April 1861 Jefferson Davis told the Confederate Congress that the North threatened “property worth thousands of millions of dollars.” That was his reason to leave, not an asking price.

Abraham Lincoln tried anyway. On March 14, 1862, he wrote that “less than eighty seven days cost of this war would, at the same price, pay for all in Delaware, Maryland, District of Columbia, Kentucky, and Missouri.” The price was $400 per person, paid in bonds. Twenty of their 28 congressmen said no. They “were not willing to impose a tax on our people sufficient to pay the interest.” Only Washington, D.C., got a buyout. In February 1865 Lincoln drafted one more offer, for the rebel states. His own cabinet voted it down.

Freedom came through war, and through enslaved people who ran to Union lines. About 179,000 Black men served in the Union army. In 1868 the Fourteenth Amendment declared “any claim for the loss or emancipation of any slave” to be “illegal and void.” The sellers wouldn’t sell. The buyers wouldn’t pay. The war settled it instead.
Lesson IV · New York bet on slave cotton, then bankrolled its destruction.
Slavery’s money didn’t stop at the Mason-Dixon line.
What 17 major civil wars left behind, best outcomes first
— = Doesn’t apply: country split

The four tests. One country: no region broke away. Kept its government: constitution and elections survived. Losers back in: could vote and hold office within 15 years. No second war: not within 50 years.
1 of 17 civil wars here ended with the country passing all four tests. It’s the United States.
* If you count only white Southerners. After federal troops left in 1877, Black Southerners were pushed out of voting and office. By 1910 almost none could vote.

Civil wars rarely leave a country whole and free. Regions split off, as in Pakistan, Sudan and Yugoslavia, or the winner rules alone, as in Russia and Spain. Of countries that had a civil war from 1945 to 2009, 57% had another (Barbara Walter). The United States came out whole, kept its constitution and never fought a second one. By 1873 the Confederacy’s own vice president was back in Congress. The price of that welcome is the rest of this story. The chart is a selection of major wars, not a full count, and most death tolls are disputed.

Sources: Walter, World Bank WDR background paper (2012); Toft, Securing the Peace (2010); Hacker, Civil War History (2011); National Park Service, “A Time of Reckoning”; Britannica; Payne, The Spanish Civil War (2012); Campbell, Council on Foreign Relations. Full case notes in the receipts.

Charles Sumner, later one of the Senate’s fiercest opponents of slavery, attacked the alliance of “the lords of the lash and the lords of the loom.” Mills in Lowell, Massachusetts, made cheap “negro cloth” to sell back to plantations. Northern insurers wrote policies on enslaved people: from 1845 to 1848 the Nautilus company of New York, which later became New York Life, wrote about 485 of them. Aetna sold them in the 1850s, and in 2000 it apologized.

By one estimate from the period, Southerners owed Northern creditors about $200 million when the war came, three-quarters of it to New York. When the South began to leave, more than 40,000 New York merchants petitioned for a compromise that would have protected slavery in the Constitution permanently. Mayor Fernando Wood proposed that New York City leave the Union too.

What the merchants feared was unpaid debts and lost customers. Then Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter, and New York changed sides fast. That year Northern banks lent the government $150 million. After the war, Southern cotton came back, grown by sharecroppers who often owed their whole crop before it was picked. Northern money wasn’t loyal to slavery. It was loyal to cotton, whoever picked it.
Lesson V · The “happy slave” was an argument before it was a memory.

The smiling, faithful slave didn’t start as nostalgia. It started as a debate strategy. By the 1830s abolitionists were flooding Congress with petitions. On February 6, 1837, Sen. John C. Calhoun of South Carolina told the Senate that slavery was, “instead of an evil, a good—a positive good.”

Then the defenders found numbers. The 1840 census reported very high rates of insanity among free Black people in the North. It was wrong. In January 1844 a Massachusetts doctor, Edward Jarvis, showed that the census had listed 133 “coloured lunatics and idiots” in Worcester who were actually “the white patients in the state hospital.”

Three months later Calhoun, now secretary of state, cited the census to the British minister to argue that freed Black people sank into “vice and pauperism... deafness, blindness, insanity and idiocy.” The numbers had already been challenged in print. No record shows whether Calhoun knew.

CAUGHT IN PRINT. The 1840 census listed 133 insane “coloured” people in Worcester, Mass., who were actually “the white patients in the state hospital.” A doctor exposed the error in January 1844. Three months later, Calhoun cited the census to Britain. No record shows whether he knew. Illustration.

After Uncle Tom’s Cabin in 1852, slavery’s defenders answered with 20 to 30 “anti-Tom” novels about kind masters and childlike slaves. The stage version was mostly Northern: the first full minstrel show opened in New York in 1843. Formerly enslaved writers answered in their own names. Frederick Douglass and Harriet Jacobs described whippings, sales and families torn apart. The war didn’t create the contented slave. It gave it a new job.

blocks.title: Callout · Saint-Domingue, 1791–1804: Haiti is why the “happy slave” story had to exist

blocks.text: The slave revolt that won scared the South for sixty years

In 1791, enslaved people in France’s richest colony rose up. Napoleon sent an army to take it back (how he got the power to send it is on p. 66). The rebels beat that army. In 1804 these formerly enslaved people founded Haiti, the only country ever born from a slave revolt.
American slaveholders saw that it could happen here. So they told a story in which it couldn’t: happy slaves don’t revolt.
Washington refused to recognize Haiti until 1862, after the South had left Congress.
Lesson VI · ◆ The Price of Peace · The Lost Cause found a Northern audience already half-persuaded.
Plenty of white Northerners opposed slavery and still didn’t want Black neighbors, and they said so at the ballot box.

items: Indiana, 1851: voters banned Black people from moving into the state, 113,828 to 21,873.
New York, 1860: voters kept a $250 property requirement for Black voters only. On the same ballot, they voted for Lincoln.
Illinois, 1862: mid-war, voters banned Black migration, Black voting and Black officeholding.
Ohio and Kansas, 1867: voters rejected the vote for Black men.

blocks.text: Lincoln carried some of this too. In August 1862 he urged five Black leaders to lead an emigration to Central America. He also changed. The final Emancipation Proclamation dropped colonization and invited Black men into the army.

The North was never one audience. Radical Republicans wrote the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. But historians such as David Blight and Nina Silber argue that this split made the Lost Cause easy to sell up North. It didn’t have to change white Northerners’ minds about race. It only had to tell them they could stop arguing about the war.

blocks.text: Lesson VII · ◆ The Price of Peace · Reconstruction died by a hundred retreats, not one secret deal.
In 1865 four million people were suddenly free, with no land and no money, and Northern voters wanted their sons home.

The first promise was land. Gen. William T. Sherman’s Special Field Order No. 15 set aside coastal land in Georgia and South Carolina for freed families, in 40-acre plots. Then President Andrew Johnson began pardoning Confederates, and in the fall of 1865 most of the Sherman land went back to its old owners. Freedmen on Edisto Island wrote: “We were promised Homestead’s by the government.” They signed off: “Landless, Homeless. Voteless.”

There were real limits. Sherman’s order had no law behind it. And Congress fought Johnson hard: it passed a Civil Rights Act over his veto, impeached him, and in 1867 Black men across the South began to vote. That was more than Britain or Brazil ever did for freed people. The story is how much of it was given back.

blocks.text: SIGNED, AND TAKEN BACK. By June 5, 1866, President Andrew Johnson had granted 12,652 special pardons to former Confederates. In the fall of 1865 most of the land Gen. Sherman set aside for freed families went back to its old owners. Illustration.

Most Union volunteers were home by 1867. In 1871 federal prosecutors broke the Ku Klux Klan in South Carolina. More than 600 men were detained, but the courts could handle only a few, and 1,188 cases were still waiting. The attorney general cut back, citing the cost and a growing feeling among white voters that Washington was meddling. In 1873 the government offered clemency. A financial panic followed. The Supreme Court narrowed the new amendments, ruling after the Colfax Massacre that the Fourteenth “adds nothing to the rights of one citizen as against another.” In 1877 federal troops pulled back from the statehouses in South Carolina and Louisiana. It’s often called a secret deal, but no written evidence of one has ever been found.

The rest followed in the open. “We met here to establish the supremacy of the white race,” a delegate told Louisiana’s 1898 constitutional convention. Black voter registration fell from 130,344 to 5,320 in three years. No one signed Reconstruction away in a single room. It was given up one reasonable-sounding retreat at a time, and Black Southerners paid for every one.

blocks.title: The 1920 rulebook, in its own words

blocks.text: “Reject a book that says the South fought to hold her slaves.”
“Reject a book that speaks of the slaveholder of the South as cruel and unjust to his slaves.”
A Measuring Rod to Test Text Books, prepared at the request of the United Confederate Veterans, 1920. Compare Mississippi’s 1861 declaration on the feature’s first page.
Lesson VIII · The veterans commissioned a grading rubric for history books.

Peace between white Northerners and white Southerners needed a shared story. The Confederacy’s veterans volunteered to write it. Edward Pollard named the movement in his 1866 book The Lost Cause. In 1868 he wrote plainly that the war’s “true question... was the supremacy of the white race.”

Then they went after the schools. In 1899 a committee of Virginia Confederate veterans declared every Northern school history it had seen “unfit for use in Southern schools.” One section of its report was titled “Slavery not the Cause of the War.”
In 1904 a Texas chapter of the United Daughters of the Confederacy printed a catechism for children. “How were the slaves treated?” it asked. “With great kindness and care in nearly all cases.”

GRADED. The 1920 rulebook told schools to “Reject a book that says the South fought to hold her slaves.” It asked librarians to mark failing books “Unjust to the South.” No marked book has turned up. Illustration.

In 1920 came the rulebook. Mildred Lewis Rutherford wrote A Measuring Rod to Test Text Books “At the Request of the United Confederate Veterans.” It asked librarians to write “Unjust to the South” on the title page of every book that failed. No marked book has turned up. One of the men who approved it, the North Carolina millionaire Julian Carr, had boasted in a 1913 speech that he once “horse-whipped a negro wench, until her skirts hung in shreds.”
Lesson IX · ◆ The Price of Peace · The “happy slave” was sold in stores and carved in stone.

After the war, the contented slave found a bigger market, much of it up North. In 1884 the New York magazine Century printed “Marse Chan,” narrated by a formerly enslaved man: “Dem wuz good ole times, marster.” Northern readers loved it.

SOLD, THEN SET IN STONE. In the 1890s a South Carolina cotton mill owner paid for a monument “Dedicated to the faithful slaves.” In 1923 the Senate passed a bill for another one in Washington. Black women organized against it, and it died in the House. Illustration.

Then the image went on the shelf. In 1889 a Missouri businessman named his pancake mix Aunt Jemima, after a minstrel song. At the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair, Nancy Green, born enslaved in Kentucky, played the character. Her plantation backstory was ad copy.

blocks.text: It went into stone too. In Fort Mill, South Carolina, a cotton mill owner paid for an 1890s monument “Dedicated to the faithful slaves.” In 1923 the U.S. Senate passed a bill for a monument in Washington “in memory of the faithful colored mammies of the South.” Its House champion said the enslaved had “desired no change in their condition of life.” Black women organized against it. “The Black Mammy had no home life,” Mary Church Terrell wrote. The bill died in the House.

In 1931 the Daughters and the Sons of Confederate Veterans dedicated a stone at Harpers Ferry to Heyward Shepherd, a Black man killed by John Brown’s raiders, as an example of “the character and faithfulness of thousands of negroes.”
Shepherd was a free man.

The Heyward Shepherd stone at Harpers Ferry, dedicated in 1931 by the United Daughters of the Confederacy and the Sons of Confederate Veterans. It was promoted as a memorial to faithful slaves. Photo: National Park Service.

At the dedication Pearl Tatten, music director at nearby Storer College, a school for Black students, spoke from the same platform. Black Americans, she said, were moving forward “not in the spirit of the black mammy but in the spirit of new freedom and rising youth.”

Freed people had left their own record. For decades after the war, they placed “Information Wanted” ads searching for mothers, husbands and children who had been sold away. Villanova University’s Last Seen project had digitized more than 900 by 2017.
Lesson X · ◆ The Price of Peace · Virginia put it in the state textbooks until 1972.
Which brings the story back to that 1957 schoolbook.

In 1950 Virginia’s legislature created a commission to write new history textbooks. The seventh-grade author was told to “make every seventh grader aspire to the colonnaded mansion; and if he can’t get there make him happy in the cabin.” The book said: “Life among the Negroes of Virginia in slavery times was generally happy.” The books arrived in 1956 and 1957, the same years Virginia launched “Massive Resistance” against school integration. The state dropped them in 1972.
Virginia’s state history books arrived in 1956–57. Every public school had to use them until 1972.

Even the best evidence got bent. In the 1930s government writers interviewed more than 2,000 formerly enslaved people. Those interviews are real testimony. But who asked the questions shaped the answers.

blocks.title: How to read a source · Who was asking?

blocks.text: In the 1930s, government interviewers asked formerly enslaved people about their lives. The historian Paul Escott compared the answers by who did the asking.
26-point gap: said their food under slavery had been good
An elderly Black Southerner in the 1930s had good reasons to be careful with a white stranger. A source can be honest and still be shaped by who is listening.
The polls have moved. A 2023 YouGov survey, worded differently from Pew’s, found 56 percent of Americans said the war was mainly about slavery.
Lesson XI · ◆ The Price of Peace · Peace had a price, and a story to go with it.
The country couldn’t buy its way out of slavery. It fought its way out. Then it faced a problem no rubric could solve: how to make one nation again out of the people who had fought.

Every real option cost something. Holding the South down cost money, troops and votes that Northern voters didn’t want to spend. Letting go cost Black Southerners their land, their ballots and often their lives. The country let go, one step at a time.

Historians such as David Blight argue that the happy slave made that choice feel like no choice at all. It let white Northerners and white Southerners honor each other’s dead without anyone owing anyone an apology. The people left out of that reunion were the four million the war had freed.

blocks.title: The strongest case against this story

blocks.text: This wasn’t a conspiracy. It was grief, money, exhaustion and a country that wanted to be done. The first Confederate monuments went up in cemeteries, built by women burying their dead. Union veterans had their own textbook committee. Many white Southerners who wrote about loyal slaves believed every word. Historians such as Gaines Foster and Caroline Janney describe a mass culture, not a command center. And the hardest choices of Reconstruction had no good answers: keeping an army in the South for decades would have been costly and unpopular. Why weigh this: it’s mostly right, and our research found no master plan. The catch is that sincere belief and open choices still had authors. The rulebook that said “Reject a book that says the South fought to hold her slaves” was written for veterans of a Confederacy whose leaders had put slavery in writing in 1861. The people who paid for the peace were never asked.
Lesson XII · So why did the pleasant story win?

One reading says it won by accident: tired white Americans wanted to hear it. Another says it won on purpose, because committees, publishers and lawmakers pushed it. The record supports some of both, and it was challenged all along. In 1915 Carter G. Woodson founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History, and the NAACP protested The Birth of a Nation. In 1935 W. E. B. Du Bois called the textbooks “a deliberate attempt so to change the facts of history that the story will make pleasant reading for Americans.”

blocks.title: SIDE EYE · Sidebar: How to lose a war and win the exam

blocks.text: A study guide, approved by the losing side.

items: Step 1: Grade the other team’s homework. In 1899 a committee of Virginia Confederate veterans declared every Northern school history it had seen “unfit for use in Southern schools.”
Step 2: Skip the hard question. One section of their report was titled “Slavery not the Cause of the War.” The Confederacy’s leaders had put slavery in writing in 1861.
Step 3: Hand out the answer key. In 1904 a Texas UDC chapter printed a children’s catechism. Q: “How were the slaves treated?” Approved A: “With great kindness and care in nearly all cases.”
Step 4: Publish the rubric. In 1920 the Measuring Rod, written “At the Request of the United Confederate Veterans,” advised: “Reject a book that says the South fought to hold her slaves.”
Step 5: Get the state to print it. Virginia’s 1950 textbook commission told its seventh-grade author to make students “happy in the cabin.” The books stayed in use until 1972.

Infographic: “One Country Again?” (1 of 17), p. 37. What it tests. Each war on the chart is scored on four questions: (1) Did the country stay one country, with no breakaway within about 30 years? (2) Did it keep its constitutional order and elections (amendments allowed)? (3) Were the losers back in politics within about 15 years? (4) Was there no second war between the same sides within 50 years?

The United States. One country: yes. Constitutional order: yes (the 1864 election was held; the 13th–15th Amendments). Losers back in politics: yes for white Southerners only (Amnesty Act, 1872; Alexander Stephens, the Confederacy’s vice president, was back in Congress by 1873). Black Southerners were pushed out of politics after 1877 (National Park Service, “A Time of Reckoning”). No second war: yes. Deaths: about 750,000, with a range of 650,000 to 850,000 (J. David Hacker, Civil War History, 2011).

What we don’t claim. We do not say the US is the only country ever to do this. The chart is a selection of 17 major civil wars, not a full count, and most death tolls are disputed. Switzerland (1847) and Finland (1918) come closest. Switzerland replaced its Federal Treaty with a new constitution in 1848; Finland exiled Red leaders.

The base rate. Of countries that had a civil war from 1945 to 2009, 57% had another (Barbara F. Walter, World Bank World Development Report background paper, 2012). The 2011 World Development Report found that more than 90% of 2000s civil wars were in countries with a civil war in the previous 30 years.
